difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (a subset condition written as an empty set difference) applied by reading the four expressions directly, well under a minute for a prepared student.
stem:
Consider a database that includes the following relations:

Defender(*name*, *rating*, *side*, *goals*)

Forward(*name*, *rating*, *assists*, *goals*)

Team(*name*, *club*, *price*)

Which **ONE** of the following relational algebra expressions checks that every name occurring in Team appears in either Defender or Forward, where $\phi$ denotes the empty set?

solution.quick: The condition "every name in Team appears in Defender or Forward" is the subset test $\Pi_{name}(\text{Team}) \subseteq \Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}) \cup \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})$. For sets, $X \subseteq Y$ holds exactly when $X \setminus Y = \phi$, so the check is $\Pi_{name}(\text{Team}) \setminus \big(\Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}) \cup \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})\big) = \phi$, option **(C)**.

steps.title: Turn the English condition into sets
steps.body:
Write the three name sets as

$$
T = \Pi_{name}(\text{Team}), \qquad D = \Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}), \qquad F = \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward}).
$$

Projection keeps only the *name* column (and removes duplicates), so each is simply a set of names.

- "appears in either Defender or Forward" means the name is in $D$ **or** in $F$ (a name in both still qualifies), i.e. it is in $D \cup F$.
- "every name occurring in Team" means this must hold for every $n \in T$.

So the condition is

$$
\forall n \in T:\; n \in D \cup F \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T \subseteq D \cup F.
$$

steps.title: Write the subset test as an emptiness test
steps.body:
Relational algebra has no $\subseteq$ operator, but set difference gives one:

$$
X \subseteq Y \iff X \setminus Y = \phi,
$$

because $X \setminus Y$ is exactly the set of elements of $X$ that are **missing** from $Y$, i.e. the violators. If there are no violators, $X$ is contained in $Y$.

With $X = T$ and $Y = D \cup F$:

$$
T \subseteq D \cup F \iff T \setminus (D \cup F) = \phi
\iff \Pi_{name}(\text{Team}) \setminus \big(\Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}) \cup \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})\big) = \phi,
$$

which is option **(C)**.

steps.title: Test the other options on small instances
steps.body:
Let the player names be $a, b, c, d$.

| Instance | Condition $T \subseteq D \cup F$ | (A) $T \setminus (D \cap F)$ | (B) $(D \cap F) \setminus T$ | (D) $(D \cup F) \setminus T$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $T=\{a,b\},\ D=\{a\},\ F=\{b\}$ | holds | $\{a,b\} \ne \phi$ (**rejects**) | $\phi$ | $\phi$ |
| $T=\{c\},\ D=\{a\},\ F=\{b\}$ | fails ($c$ is in neither) | $\{c\} \ne \phi$ | $\phi$ (**accepts**) | $\{a,b\} \ne \phi$ |
| $T=\{a\},\ D=\{a,d\},\ F=\phi$ | holds | $\{a\} \ne \phi$ | $\phi$ | $\{d\} \ne \phi$ (**rejects**) |

- (A) really tests $T \subseteq D \cap F$ ("every Team name is **both** a defender and a forward"), which is too strict (row 1).
- (B) tests $D \cap F \subseteq T$, a different set in the wrong direction; it can accept a Team name that is nowhere else (row 2).
- (D) tests $D \cup F \subseteq T$ ("every defender and forward is in Team"), the reverse inclusion (row 3).

Only (C) agrees with the condition on every row: $\{a,b\} \setminus \{a,b\} = \phi$ (accept), $\{c\} \setminus \{a,b\} = \{c\}$ (reject), $\{a\} \setminus \{a,d\} = \phi$ (accept).

steps.title: Exhaustive check
steps.body: A Python check enumerates every choice of $T$, $D$, $F$ as subsets (of up to 3 names each) of a 5-name universe and compares each expression's "$= \phi$" result with $T \subseteq D \cup F$. Only (C) agrees on every instance; (A), (B) and (D) each fail on some instance. The answer is **(C)**.

solution.teaching:
**Relational algebra works on sets of tuples.** Projection $\Pi_{A}(R)$ keeps only the columns in $A$ and removes duplicate rows. Union ($\cup$), intersection ($\cap$) and difference ($\setminus$ or $-$) are the ordinary set operations, but they need **union-compatible** inputs: the same number of attributes with matching domains. Defender has *side* where Forward has *assists*, and Team has a different schema again, so these relations cannot be combined directly. Projecting all three onto *name* makes them compatible: each becomes a one-column set of names.

**Translating words into set operations.**

| English | Set operation |
|---|---|
| in X **or** Y (either one, or both) | $X \cup Y$ |
| in X **and** Y (both) | $X \cap Y$ |
| in X but **not** in Y | $X \setminus Y$ |
| **every** element of X is in Y | $X \subseteq Y$, i.e. $X \setminus Y = \phi$ |

The last line is the key idea. Relational algebra cannot say "for all" directly, so a universal condition is checked by computing its **counterexamples** and requiring that there are none. $X \setminus Y$ lists the members of $X$ that are not in $Y$; an empty result means every member of $X$ is in $Y$.

**Direction matters.** The set being quantified over ("every name occurring in Team") must be on the **left** of the difference. Swapping the sides checks the reverse inclusion, a different constraint.

**Where you meet this in practice.** It is exactly how a referential-integrity (foreign-key) constraint is stated: every value in the referencing column must appear in the referenced column, i.e. $\Pi_{fk}(R) \setminus \Pi_{pk}(S) = \phi$. In SQL the same test is "`SELECT name FROM Team EXCEPT (SELECT name FROM Defender UNION SELECT name FROM Forward)` returns no rows".

**Back to this question.** "Every name in Team" puts $\Pi_{name}(\text{Team})$ on the left, and "either Defender or Forward" is the union $\Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}) \cup \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})$ on the right. That gives option (C).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $T \setminus (D \cap F) = \phi$ means $T \subseteq D \cap F$: every Team name must be **both** a defender and a forward. That is stricter than the condition asked. With $T=\{a,b\}$, $D=\{a\}$, $F=\{b\}$ the condition holds, yet $D \cap F = \phi$ and the expression gives $\{a,b\} \ne \phi$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $(D \cap F) \setminus T = \phi$ means $D \cap F \subseteq T$: every player listed as both defender and forward is in Team. It says nothing about Team names outside $D \cap F$. With $T=\{c\}$, $D=\{a\}$, $F=\{b\}$, name $c$ is in neither relation, yet $D \cap F = \phi$ makes the expression $\phi$, so the check wrongly passes.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $T \setminus (D \cup F)$ is the set of Team names found in neither Defender nor Forward, i.e. the violators. It is empty exactly when $T \subseteq D \cup F$, which is the stated condition. This matches the official key.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $(D \cup F) \setminus T = \phi$ means $D \cup F \subseteq T$: every defender and forward is in Team. That is the reverse inclusion. With $T=\{a\}$, $D=\{a,d\}$, $F=\phi$ the condition holds but the expression gives $\{d\} \ne \phi$; with $T=\{a,c\}$, $D=\{a\}$, $F=\phi$ the condition fails but the expression gives $\phi$.

solution.shortcut: "Every $X$ is in $Y$" $\iff X \setminus Y = \phi$. Put the set after "every" (Team) on the **left** of $\setminus$, and read "either … or" as $\cup$. Only (C) has Team on the left and $\cup$ on the right.
solution.commonTrap: Reversing the difference and picking (D), which checks that every defender and forward is in Team rather than the other way round. A second trap is reading "either Defender or Forward" as "both", which leads to the intersection in (A).

answerVerification.notes: The condition is the set inclusion Π_name(Team) ⊆ Π_name(Defender) ∪ Π_name(Forward), and X ⊆ Y holds exactly when X ∖ Y = ϕ, which is option C. A Python check enumerates all choices of T, D, F (subsets of up to 3 names from a 5-name universe) and confirms that only expression C matches T ⊆ D ∪ F on every instance, while A, B and D each fail on some instance. This agrees with official key C.
